skin.setting: a mountain observatory snowed in for the season, 1957
skin.title: The Cold Light of Midnight
skin.place: Peak St. Jude Observatory, High Alps
skin.styleGuide: Moody mid-century monochrome photography, heavy wool coats, frosted glass, brass telescopes, bakelite dials, and harsh mountain shadows.

rooms.name: the Grand Gallery
rooms.description: A long, draughty corridor lined with framed celestial charts, connecting the wings of the mountain station.

rooms.name: the Archive Library
rooms.description: Floor-to-ceiling shelves of astronomical logs and star catalogues surrounding a heavy oak reading table.

rooms.name: the Radio Room
rooms.description: A cramped station filled with warm glowing vacuum tubes, Morse keys, and transceivers crackling with mountain static.

rooms.name: the Sky Terrace
rooms.description: An open-air stone platform overlooking the frozen abyss, surrounded by iron railings crusted in rime.

rooms.name: the Optical Workshop
rooms.description: Benches littered with brass fittings, lens-grinding powders, calipers, and drafting schematics.

rooms.name: the Dome Chamber
rooms.description: The massive circular rotunda housing the great refracting telescope beneath a split copper dome.

rooms.name: the Generator Vault
rooms.description: A subterranean chamber vibrating with the low, steady thrum of a heavy diesel dynamo.

people.name: Dr. Kenneth Adler
people.bio: A meticulous researcher who spent decades pursuing a tenure post that slipped through his fingers. He believes the observatory's prestige belongs entirely to his foundational work.
people.voice: Formal, clipped, and deeply resentful of interruptions.
people.motive: Professor Sterling had prepared a formal report to strip Adler of his research grant and credit for the comet discovery.
people.portrait: A severe middle-aged man with sharp spectacles, receding hair, and an impeccably buttoned tweed waistcoat.

people.name: Vera Lindqvist
people.bio: A hardened field scientist stationed at the peak to record extreme atmospheric data. She rarely mingles with the academic staff and keeps her thoughts guarded.
people.voice: Direct, dry, and unconcerned with polite niceties.
people.motive: Sterling threatened to falsify her weather records to hide his negligence in an earlier expedition disaster.
people.portrait: A sharp-eyed woman with wind-chapped cheeks, hair pulled into a tight bun, wearing a thick wool jumper.

people.name: Gregory Fox
people.bio: The practical mind responsible for keeping the dome mechanism and generators running through brutal alpine blizzards. He considers the academic staff arrogant and detached from reality.
people.motive: Sterling had discovered financial discrepancies in Fox's equipment requisitions and planned to dismiss him without pension.
people.portrait: A burly man in grease-stained canvas overalls with calloused hands and a heavy stubble.

people.name: Dr. Clara Meyer
people.bio: A brilliant young theoretician sent to verify the observatory's contentious new spectroscopic data. Her relentless questioning quickly irritated the older staff.
people.motive: Sterling had blocked her upcoming monograph publication by claiming her theoretical models were derivative of his own.
people.portrait: A young woman with intense dark eyes, wearing a dark knitted cardigan and holding a notepad.

people.name: Arthur Vance
people.bio: The station's longtime custodian who knows every crawlspace, keyhole, and draft in the observatory. He has quietly endured years of condescension from the director.
people.motive: Sterling was preparing to replace Vance before the winter ended, leaving him destitute in the mountain village.
people.portrait: An elderly, weathered man with heavy jowls, a heavy ring of iron keys, and a faded flannel work coat.

people.name: Professor Donald Sterling
people.bio: The imperious director of Peak St. Jude Observatory whose tyrannical rule earned him many enemies. His body was found beneath the great telescope.
people.portrait: A stern, silver-haired gentleman in a bespoke tailored suit with a pocket watch chain across his vest.

silence: "I have accounted for what I know, and speculation does not interest me," Dr. Kenneth Adler says coldly.
"I've said all I'm going to say about that stretch of time," Vera Lindqvist remarks.
"Nothing more to tell on that score, Inspector," Gregory Fox mutters, wiping his wrench.
"I have no further observations to offer regarding that period," Dr. Clara Meyer states briskly.
"I didn't see anything else worth mentioning, sir," Arthur Vance replies softly.
Donald Sterling lies motionless under the observatory dome, silent forever.
skin.briefing: A ferocious blizzard has completely severed the Peak St. Jude Observatory from the valley below, trapping five researchers and staff members inside the stone compound. Shortly after midnight, the tyrannical director, Professor Donald Sterling, was found dead on the brass deck of the Dome Chamber. One among the remaining five is a murderer who will lie to conceal their movements, while the innocent have recounted their steps with strict precision. The mountain telephone lines are down, leaving you to retrace the hours and uncover the truth.
skin.scene: A towering stone observatory perched on a jagged alpine summit under a swirling blizzard, warm yellow light spilling from slit windows onto fresh drifts of snow.
skin.summingUp:
The frost has crept across the heavy glass, casting long, sharp silhouettes between the brass telescopes and the quiet bakelite dials. We have stood here in our heavy wool coats waiting for the mountain shadows to yield what happened to Professor Donald Sterling, but the sequence of facts is already stark and undeniable.

To begin with, Card 5 narrows down when the murder happened, which immediately eliminates six o'clock and midnight from our timeline. Following that, Card 17 narrows down the hours even further, proving without doubt that the murder was not at eleven o'clock.

Next, we know with certainty that the killer and Professor Donald Sterling were both present in the Dome Chamber when it happened. That crucial presence clears Gregory Fox of suspicion, and it establishes that the murder was not at ten o'clock. By that very same rule—that the killer and the victim shared this room at the fateful hour—the murder was not at nine o'clock.

From there, the web tightens. Because Vera Lindqvist and Arthur Vance cannot both have been innocent, Dr. Kenneth Adler and Dr. Clara Meyer are entirely in the clear. Returning to the movements within the Dome Chamber, the necessity of both the killer and Sterling being here together proves that the murder was not at eight o'clock.

Finally, because there is simply no way for Arthur Vance to have been innocent, Vera Lindqvist is in the clear. That leaves only one man and one final hour. It was Arthur Vance who struck down Professor Sterling here in the Dome Chamber at seven o'clock, desperate to prevent Sterling from replacing him before winter's end and leaving him destitute in this freezing mountain village.
